frantic longing. Because of his physical condition and the social mores of Boston, he couldn't have the physical intimacy he desperately craved.
So he retreats to the isolated woods and entirely eroticizes the landscape. He writes passionately about the aeros of a delicate
damsel landing on his thigh. He is projecting his deeply frustrated human desires onto oblivious bugs and trees simply because they
cannot reject him. It's a massive ego trip disguised as high-minded naturalism. That is an incredibly cynical reading of a man who is clearly experiencing a
profound, albeit painful, spiritual awakening. You are reducing his genuine connection to the sublime down to mere sexual frustration.
I argue that William actually achieved a rare genuine connection to the forest's deep geological time.
When he meticulously paints the specific structural fractures in the ice on the lake or spends days trying to capture the exact flat gray of
an impending snowstorm, he is seeing the physical world with a hyper clarity that most humans rushing through their lives never achieve.
But is it genuine? I think it is. He is genuinely trying to strip away the anthropocentric ego.
The fact that he struggles with it, the fact that he realizes how impossible it is, doesn't mean the attempt is purely selfish.
It means he is one of the few humans who actually recognizes how hard it is to truly see nature for what it is rather than what we want it to be.
But look at what happens when another human actually enters his pristine sanctuary. His former nurse, Anna, comes out to the wilderness to save him from starvation.
And she nurses him back to health. She falls deeply in love with him. And what does she do? She realizes she has to secretly destroy a letter from Nash to
keep William isolated and entirely for herself. Yeah, that gets messy. It gets so messy. The messy, jealous, needy human drama completely infects
and destroys his pure wilderness retreat. He ends up just as entangled in deceit and human messiness in the middle of the woods as he ever was in the drawing rooms of
Boston. He can't escape human nature by hiding in the trees. And ultimately, what happens to all those painstakingly crafted paintings?
What is the final fate of his desperate attempt to perfectly capture the essence of the woods on canvas? The woods swallow his art just like they swallow
the apples and the bones. Decades later, his brilliant paintings are just
dusty, forgotten relics shoved in the dark attic of the yellow house,
completely divorced from the living, breathing, constantly changing forest he tried to freeze in oil paint.
The force doesn't care about his brilliant compositions or his transcendentalist philosophies. The dirt outlasts the canvas.
The place, not the people, is the true protagonist. Which brings us to the forces that the forest actually does care about.
The biological forces that reshape the entire landscape without a single philosophical thought. Right?
Which forces us to ask a terrifying question. How do the absolute smallest microscopic invaders execute the most
massive devastating shifts in ecological power? Let's zoom in on this scene. We are no longer looking at humans.
